newsitem.title: CHINA: China limits sugar imports to lift prices.
newsitem.headline: China limits sugar imports to lift prices.

text.p: China's decision to extend a ban on imports of sugar into 1997 was aimed at boosting prices hard hit by smuggling and protecting sugar factories from further losses, officials said on Friday.

China's existing ban on imports of sugar not for processing and re-export would remain in place in 1997, the Economic Information Daily on Thursday quoted an official of the State Planning Commission as saying.

"The main reason for the ban is because of mass smuggling in the past that has led to an oversupply of sugar and severely hit the sugar industry," an official of the China National Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Import and Export Corp (COFCO) said.
"Sugar prices have failed to recover, so the government wants to limit imports for another year," the official, who declined to be identified, said by telephone.

COFCO imported no sugar apart from product for processing and re-export in 1996 and had no plans to resume imports in 1997, he said. He said he had yet to receive official notification that the ban would continue into 1997.
Agricultural officials quoted by the Economic Information Daily said that continuation of the ban was meant to stabilise sugar output.

The Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation suspended imports of sugar in 1996 to curb huge losses by the sugar industry in the wake of rampant smuggling and oversupply. Sugar imports for processing are still allowed.
"Excessive imports will hit the domestic sugar industry because domestic production costs are higher than overseas," said an official of the China Sugar and Wine Co (Group).
Sluggish sugar prices resulting from illegal imports in the past two years have forced many of China's sugar factories in major producing provinces sharply into the red.

Sugar smuggling -- often disguised as imports for processing and re-exporting but sold in domestic markets for higher profits -- soared amid domestic shortages in 1994. Officials have said about 2.0 million tonnes entered China illegally in 1995.

Sugar prices dipped when the current crushing season started in October, the China Sugar official said. The wholesale price in Beijing had fallen to 4,300 yuan ($518) per tonne this week, lower than last month, he said, but gave no comparative figures.

Ex-factory prices in the southern producing provinces fell to as low as 3,800-3,900 yuan per tonne recently, the COFCO official said. Some factories had to sell sugar at very low prices to obtain enough cash to pay farmers for their product.
China's sugar output in the 1996/97 season (October/April) was forecast at 6.6 million tonnes, an increase of 380,000 tonnes from the previous season, sugar officials have said.

China's total sugar supply for the season was estimated at 7.3 million tonnes, with 700,000 tonnes imported from Cuba in 1996 and 1997, the Economic Information Daily said. China consumes about 7.0 million tonnes of sugar a year.

China's sugar exports were 616,539 tonnes in the first 11 months, up 112.9 percent compared with the year-ago period, customs figures showed. Imports slumped 55.6 percent to 1.16 million tonnes in the first 11 months.
"In the first half of 1997, general trade in sugar will be strictly banned, although some imports may be allowed in the second half," the COFCO official said.
